description: Looking for those who can contribute to Ai development in Healthcare sector
summary:
On a long mission, nobody else is watching your body the way a doctor would at home. Radiation, months in a small cabin, and living without normal gravity can quietly change your immune system, your bones, your heart, and how you feel day to day. We built ASTRIA so an astronaut can see that happening in themselves, before it becomes a crisis.

ASTRIA pulls together the signals already around them: a wearable, a short daily check-in, and readings from the cabin. It compares those signals with that person’s own normal. If sleep is slipping, bones are losing ground, or the heart is working harder than it should, ASTRIA says so in plain language and suggests what to do next. That might be a change in exercise, light, or food, or a reason to call for a medical review.

It matters because help from Earth can be hours away, or farther. The person on the mission has to notice first. ASTRIA is there so they do not have to guess.
details:
ASTRIA is a health check-in for a person on a long mission. There is no account. In about a minute, the astronaut records sleep, mood, energy, meals, resting heart rate, loading exercise, how the air feels, and a few plain signs such as a sore throat, dizziness, irritability, or loneliness. The notes stay in the browser.

ASTRIA compares that day with the person’s own recent days, not with a generic chart. It reads four areas that long missions put under pressure: the immune system, bones and muscles, the heart, and mood. Each area comes back in words first: Steady, Watch, or Needs a step. Then it offers one next action the person can take on board, such as talking with a crewmate for ten minutes, doing a short loading session, protecting sleep, eating a real meal, or asking for a medical review. A sample week is built in so the voice is visible before anyone types. That week is invented. A real check-in replaces it. ASTRIA does not diagnose.

The benefit is early notice. Radiation, months in a small cabin, altered gravity, and closed air can change the body quietly. On a long mission the crew member is often the first person who can see that. ASTRIA turns a scattered day into one clear status and one concrete step, before a small change stacks into a crisis. The intended impact is a calmer, earlier response: the astronaut knows what changed, what to do tonight, and when a feeling is serious enough to ask for a real review.

The app is written in HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. It is a static site, with Firebase Hosting configured so it can be published without a login. The project is public at github.com/skysmiletech/astrix. No special hardware is required. Check-ins are stored only on the device.

NASA records used in the app are a saved set of DONKI solar energetic particle events, Open Science Data Repository studies OSD-575 and OSD-656 from the Inspiration4 crew, and the Human Research Program risk areas that shape the four cards. Public astronaut records are not a live stream of heart rate or mood, so personal check-ins are the astronaut’s own entries, clearly separate from those studies.

The creative choice is the voice and the limit. Instead of a dense medical dashboard, ASTRIA speaks in short human sentences and asks for only one action. The team considered distance from Earth, the need to compare a person with their own baseline, privacy, the difference between a prompt and a diagnosis, and the duty to say where Super Intelligence tools were used. Grok, in Cursor, drafted the code and the words. Cursor image generation made the illustrations, each marked ai-generated in small type. No space-agency logos or mission identifiers were used.
